passage:
Subject: please read when you're alone

Shalini Didi,
I told Amma and Appa last week that I got the campus offer from the logistics company. I didn't. I didn't even clear the second round. And the backlogs from third semester are still there; I've been saying they're cleared since June.
Every Sunday call, Appa asks about joining dates, and I invent another detail. I've started dreading the phone. Yesterday Amma told the whole family group about "Kamal's job", and I sat on my hostel bed feeling sick.
I can't keep this going till July. I'm more scared of their faces than of anything else. Can you be on the call with me this Sunday when I tell them? I'll say it myself. I just don't want to be alone for it.
Kamal

qa.q: What did Kamal tell Amma and Appa last week?
qa.a: Kamal told them about getting the campus offer from the logistics company.

qa.q: What is Kamal most afraid of?
qa.a: Kamal is most scared of seeing the parents' disappointment, which shows in dreading the phone and feeling sick after the family group message.

qa.q: Which step in the email is a wise one, and why?
qa.a: Asking Shalini Didi to be on the call while Kamal tells the truth is wise, because support makes it easier to stop the lies before July.

qa.q: What might it be like for Amma and Appa to hear the truth on Sunday?
qa.a: They may feel shocked and disappointed, especially after telling the family, but hearing it from Kamal now is better than finding out later.

grounding: A student who claimed a job offer while failing admits to Shalini Didi how fear of disappointing the parents has turned the story into a trap.

passage:
My first year of pharmacy college? A performance, honestly. I'm Minakshi, and I failed two papers in the first semester. On the phone I told my parents I'd scored eighty-five percent. My father handed out sweets at his shop for "our topper daughter". After that I couldn't take it back.
In the second semester I had to keep inventing: a certificate that was "still being printed", a professor who had "praised me in class". I stopped going home for festivals, because I couldn't look at the sweets box.
It ended when the college posted the result sheet home. My mother called, very quiet, and asked, "Why didn't you trust us?" I cried for an hour. We're still repairing it. The failing was fixable. The story nearly wasn't.

qa.q: What score did Minakshi tell her parents she had?
qa.a: Minakshi told them she'd scored eighty-five percent.

qa.q: Why did Minakshi feel she couldn't take the lie back?
qa.a: Her father had already handed out sweets at his shop, so she felt ashamed and afraid of disappointing him in front of everyone.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could have helped earlier?
qa.a: Each lie needed another until the result sheet exposed it; telling her parents after the first semester, perhaps with a college counsellor's support, would have kept it fixable.

qa.q: How might Minakshi's mother have felt when she asked, "Why didn't you trust us?"
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and sad that her daughter couldn't tell her the truth, more than angry about the failed papers.

grounding: A young woman tells how hiding failed papers from a proud family turned into a trap that grew worse than the failure itself.
